newsitem.title: CANADA: Goodale says Japan to enforce pork import rules.
newsitem.headline: Goodale says Japan to enforce pork import rules.

text.p: Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale said on Friday that Japanese officials had pledged to enforce pork tariffs fairly.

Speaking on a conference call with journalists from Tokyo, where he is on a trade mission, Goodale said he had raised Canadian pork industry allegations about Taiwan pork shipments with Japanese Agriculture Minister Takeo Fujimoto.
"The concern about that has been duly registered and we did have a response from the Japanese indicating that they took this matter seriously," Goodale said.
"They do not want their laws, rules and regulations to be flouted and in fact most recently there had been a number of prosecutions pursued in relation to this matter," he said.

Jim Morris, president of Canada Pork International, a Canadian pork export promotion group, told the Canadian Wheat Board's Grain World Conference on March 4 that Taiwanese exporters were "submarining" pork imports into Japan with inaccurate invoicing to avoid Japan's current tariff.
"Taiwan will continue to evade the Japanese duty system through false invoicing, and the Japanese government will continue to pretend that it doesn't exist," Morris said.
Japan's total pork imports rose 12.5 percent in 1996 to 653,178 tonnes with Canada holding a 6.2 percent market share.
Goodale said the Japanese officials recognized the problem with administering their tariff system.

"This is obviously a subject of considerable sensitivity," Goodale said. "I think that point registered with my Japanese counterparts and they did indicate that most recently some particular efforts had been made to ensure that enforcement of the regime was being applied on a more even-handed basis than had been the case in the past," he said.
Goodale said Fujimoto had made no indication of whether the pork import tariff would be extended beyond this June.

"But if one looks at the formula that they apply...it would appear likely that some snap-back provision would continue to be in place on the basis of the obvious arithmetic that applies to the formula," Goodale said.

"That's a layman's judgement looking in from the outside, but on the basis of the volume numbers that are there on the record, the likelihood of the safeguard regime being removed in the short term does not appear to be very strong," he said.

Japan's "safeguard" duties, which are meant to control the volume of pork imports, are permitted under world trade rules. The measures, in effect since last July, have increased average prices of pork imports by 24 percent.
Japan on March 3 said the duties, which were due to end on April 1, would be extended through at least June.
Canada's overall pork exports in 1996 set a record at 352,688 tonnes, up 14 percent in value terms to C$1.105 billion.
